questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has had nausea, vomiting, crampy abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea since early this morning. Eighteen hours earlier she ate chicken that had been undercooked at a family barbecue. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. There is no blood in her stool.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Undercooked poultry with onset 12–48 hours later, nausea and vomiting is classic Salmonella; Campylobacter takes 48–72 hours and Staph aureus only 1–6 hours.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Poultry plus an **18 hour** incubation sits in the Salmonella window of **12–48 hours**.

elim: Also from poultry, but incubation is 48–72 hours and diarrhoea is usually bloody with a flu-like prodrome.
Follows antibiotic use, not a single food exposure.
Causes weeks of watery diarrhoea and bloating after travel, not an illness 18 hours after a meal.
Preformed toxin gives vomiting within 1–6 hours, usually without fever.

steps.x: **D. Salmonella species (non-typhoidal).** Incubation sorts the poultry bugs: Salmonella 12–48 h, Campylobacter 48–72 h.

questions.stem: A 22 year old agricultural student has bloody diarrhoea and colicky abdominal pain. Three days ago she drank unpasteurised milk on a farm visit. The day before the diarrhoea began she had headache, aching muscles and fever. Her temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 102 bpm. Her abdomen is diffusely tender.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Unpasteurised milk, a flu-like prodrome and bloody diarrhoea about 3 days later is Campylobacter jejuni.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Unpasteurised milk, **flu-like prodrome**, then **bloody** diarrhoea after **48–72 hours** = Campylobacter.

elim: Linked to reheated rice with onset within hours.
Gives non-bloody watery diarrhoea and bloating.
Typhoid gives a prolonged stepwise fever and constipation before diarrhoea, after travel to an endemic area.
Onset 1–6 hours, profuse vomiting, non-bloody diarrhoea.

steps.x: **B. Campylobacter jejuni.** Prodrome then bloody diarrhoea 2–4 days after meat, milk or untreated water = Campylobacter.

questions.stem: Three office workers develop profuse vomiting and abdominal cramps within 3 hours of sharing ham sandwiches that had been left out of the fridge all morning. Two have watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. None has a fever. One woman's pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Profuse vomiting within 1–6 hours of unrefrigerated meat or dairy is Staph aureus food poisoning from a preformed toxin.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Onset within **1–6 hours** of unrefrigerated food, vomiting dominant, afebrile.

elim: Incubation 48–72 hours with bloody diarrhoea.
Antibiotic-associated, not a point-source outbreak.
Incubation 12–48 hours, usually with fever.
Incubation of several days, with diarrhoea and right iliac fossa pain.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus aureus.** The shortest incubation (1–6 h) with vomiting = Staph aureus.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has had a fever for 9 days that has climbed a little higher each day. He returned from Dhaka 2 weeks ago. He has abdominal pain and has been constipated. His observation chart over the last few days is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Observation chart
visual.caption: Temperature rises stepwise while the pulse stays below 80 bpm.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Bloody diarrhoea from the first day
questions.e: Stepwise fever after travel to South Asia with constipation is typhoid; the pulse is inappropriately slow for the temperature (Faget sign).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: climbed a little higher each day
steps.x: Stepwise fever, South Asia, constipation = **typhoid**. Look at the pulse on the chart: it stays low as the fever climbs.

elim: Mumps, not an enteric fever.
Typhoid gives constipation first, then later diarrhoea; early bloody diarrhoea suggests Campylobacter or Shigella.
Meningism suggests meningitis.
Shingles.

steps.x: **D. Relative bradycardia.** Typhoid: stepwise fever with relative bradycardia (Faget sign).

questions.stem: A 19 year old student returns from visiting relatives in Lagos with 12 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain. She was constipated at first but now has loose stools. There are faint pink macules on her trunk and the spleen tip is palpable. Her temperature is 39.3°C and pulse rate 78 bpm. Three malaria films are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever after travel with constipation followed by diarrhoea, rose spots, splenomegaly and relative bradycardia is typhoid (Salmonella typhi).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: faint pink macules on her trunk
steps.x: Rose spots, splenomegaly, constipation then diarrhoea, and a pulse of **78** at **39.3°C** (relative bradycardia).

elim: Gives bloody diarrhoea and liver abscess, not rose spots with relative bradycardia.
Short illness with bloody diarrhoea, not 12 days of fever with splenomegaly.
Gives fever, myalgia and a blanching rash with thrombocytopenia, not constipation then diarrhoea.
Excluded by three negative films.

steps.x: **E. Typhoid fever.** Rose spots + splenomegaly + relative bradycardia after travel = typhoid.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman on a care of the elderly ward has had 7 watery stools a day for 2 days. She completed a course of ciprofloxacin for pyelonephritis 4 days ago and takes omeprazole. Her temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. Her lower abdomen is tender. Proctoscopy shows inflamed, abnormal rectal mucosa.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diarrhoea, fever and abnormal rectal mucosa after ciprofloxacin in an elderly woman on a PPI is C. difficile infection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Risk factors stack up: **age >65**, **recent antibiotic**, **PPI**, hospital setting.

elim: Gives left iliac fossa pain and fever, not profuse watery diarrhoea after antibiotics.
Sudden pain with bloody diarrhoea in vascular patients; not antibiotic-triggered.
Vomiting-predominant, short-lived; no link to antibiotics or PPI.
New UC at 83 is unlikely; the antibiotic and PPI history point to C. difficile.

steps.x: **A. Clostridioides difficile infection.** Antibiotics + PPI + age >65 + watery diarrhoea = C. difficile.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man develops C. difficile infection 10 days after a hernia repair. He received no antibiotics before or after surgery. His regular medications are amlodipine, lansoprazole, metformin, paracetamol and simvastatin. He has no history of immunosuppression.
questions.q: Which of his medications is the most likely risk factor?
questions.e: Proton pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid and are a key C. difficile risk factor alongside antibiotics, age over 65 and immunosuppression.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which of his medications is the most likely risk factor? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
No antibiotics, so look for the other drug risk factor: a **PPI**.

elim: Not a recognised C. difficile risk factor.
Can cause diarrhoea itself but does not predispose to C. difficile.
No link to C. difficile.
No link to C. difficile.

steps.x: **B. Lansoprazole.** C. difficile risk factors: antibiotics, PPIs, age >65, immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man is being treated for C. difficile infection. Over 24 hours his diarrhoea has lessened but his abdomen has become markedly distended and tender. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg. Abdominal X-ray shows a transverse colon of 8 cm diameter with mucosal thumb-printing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: A distended, dilated colon with thumb-printing and systemic toxicity in C. difficile is toxic megacolon; falling stool frequency can be a warning sign.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely complication? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Colon dilated with **thumb-printing**, patient septic and shocked.

elim: Pseudo-obstruction without colitis or systemic toxicity.
A mucosal finding on endoscopy; it does not explain an 8 cm dilated colon with shock.
Gives a coffee-bean loop in the sigmoid, not transverse dilation with thumb-printing.
Gives dilated central small bowel loops, not a dilated colon.

steps.x: **E. Toxic megacolon.** C. difficile + dilated colon with thumb-printing + toxicity = toxic megacolon.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has had profuse watery diarrhoea, bloating and foul-smelling flatulence for 3 weeks since returning from backpacking in Peru, where he drank tap water. He has lost 4 kg. Two stool cultures have been negative. He has no fever and no blood in his stool.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Weeks of watery diarrhoea with bloating and weight loss after travel, with negative stool cultures, is giardiasis causing malabsorption.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Two stool cultures have been negative
steps.x: Prolonged watery diarrhoea, **bloating**, weight loss (malabsorption), **negative cultures**.

elim: Causes bloody diarrhoea lasting days and would grow on culture.
Causes bloody dysentery.
Causes a systemic stepwise fever.
Causes a short vomiting illness within hours of food.

steps.x: **C. Giardia lamblia.** Bloating + weeks of watery diarrhoea after travel + negative cultures = Giardia.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has had weakness in both legs for 5 days that has spread to his arms. Three weeks ago he had bloody diarrhoea and fever after eating undercooked chicken. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent. Power is 3/5 in both legs. Sensation is mildly reduced in his feet.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his preceding illness?
questions.e: Ascending areflexic weakness weeks after bloody diarrhoea from chicken is Guillain-Barré syndrome triggered by Campylobacter jejuni.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his preceding illness? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Knee and ankle reflexes are absent
steps.x: Ascending weakness with **areflexia** = Guillain-Barré syndrome, after **bloody diarrhoea** from chicken.

elim: Antibiotic-associated colitis; not linked to Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Causes non-bloody diarrhoea and malabsorption.
Also from chicken, but Campylobacter is the classic trigger of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Toxin-mediated vomiting within hours.

steps.x: **A. Campylobacter jejuni.** Guillain-Barré after diarrhoea: think Campylobacter jejuni.

questions.stem: A 42 year old restaurant cook is diagnosed with typhoid fever after a trip to Karachi. Public health officers want to know how she acquired the infection so that they can advise her family.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of transmission?
o: Faeco-oral, via contaminated food or water
questions.e: Salmonella typhi spreads faeco-orally, mainly through food or water contaminated in areas of poor sanitation such as South Asia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely route of transmission? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Typhoid from South Asia: an enteric infection of **poor sanitation**.

elim: Respiratory spread, as in influenza.
Malaria and dengue, not typhoid.
Not the route for typhoid.
Lyme disease and rickettsial infections.

steps.x: **B. Faeco-oral, via contaminated food or water.** Typhoid is faeco-oral; it is notifiable, so inform public health (Public Health England guidance on notifiable GI infections).

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has had 6 episodes of watery diarrhoea a day for 4 days with lower abdominal cramps. Two weeks ago her dentist prescribed clindamycin for a dental abscess. Her temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 100 bpm. Stool microscopy shows no ova or parasites. She has never had bowel symptoms before.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Clindamycin is a high-risk antibiotic for C. difficile, which causes diarrhoea, abdominal pain and high fever; it can occur in young patients too.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Clindamycin** is one of the classic C. difficile antibiotics; fever and diarrhoea follow.

elim: New onset after an antibiotic course with fever is much more likely infective.
No travel history and onset follows antibiotics.
Does not cause fever.
Vomiting within hours of food, not days of diarrhoea after antibiotics.

steps.x: **A. Clostridioides difficile infection.** Penicillins, clindamycin, cephalosporins and ciprofloxacin all predispose to C. difficile.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has had fever for 8 days after returning from Kathmandu. He has a headache, abdominal pain and constipation. His temperature is 39.1°C and pulse rate 76 bpm. A stool culture sent 2 days ago has grown no pathogens. Malaria films are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Typhoid is systemic and bacteraemic, so blood culture is the diagnostic test; stool cultures are often negative early.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Suspected **typhoid** (fever, travel, relative bradycardia). The organism is in the **blood**.

elim: May show splenomegaly but cannot identify the organism.
Invasive and not needed to diagnose typhoid.
Stool culture is the gold standard for most infectious diarrhoea but is often negative early in typhoid.
Low yield; not the diagnostic test for typhoid.

steps.x: **B. Blood culture.** Typhoid is diagnosed with blood culture; other infectious diarrhoea with stool culture.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has had bloody diarrhoea 7 times a day for 5 days with fever and cramping. He is concerned about missing more work. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. His abdomen is mildly tender.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
questions.e: Bloody and persistent diarrhoea needs investigating, and stool culture is the gold standard for identifying the organism.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Bloody** diarrhoea with fever lasting 5 days: this is one of the reasons to investigate.

elim: Looks for complications such as toxic megacolon, not the cause.
Diagnostic for typhoid, not for bloody diarrhoea.
Not first choice in acute infective colitis.
Shows gut inflammation but not the organism.

steps.x: **E. Stool culture.** Investigate if severe, bloody, persistent or immunocompromised; the gold standard is stool culture.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer has had watery diarrhoea 5 times a day for 3 days. She has not travelled and has not had antibiotics recently. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Immunocompromise is an indication to investigate, so stool microscopy, culture and PCR is needed to find the pathogen.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
She is **immunocompromised**, so a clinical diagnosis alone is not enough.

elim: Not first line without signs of a complication.
Tests pancreatic exocrine function, not infection.
Invasive; stool testing comes first.
Reasonable for mild cases in healthy people, but she is immunocompromised.

steps.x: **E. Stool microscopy, culture and PCR.** Most infectious diarrhoea is a clinical diagnosis, except in severe, bloody, persistent or immunocompromised cases.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 3 days. He takes ramipril and furosemide. He is drowsy and his mucous membranes are dry. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 94/60 mmHg and capillary refill time 4 seconds.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: In a dehydrated older patient on an ACE inhibitor and diuretic, U&Es look for acute kidney injury and electrolyte disturbance.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Signs of **dehydration** with drugs that harm the kidneys and electrolytes.

elim: Does not assess dehydration or kidney function.
Not indicated in acute gastroenteritis.
Do not guide fluid and electrolyte replacement.
Not urgent in acute dehydration.

steps.x: **E. Urea and electrolytes.** First-line bloods in infective diarrhoea: U&Es for dehydration, and FBC.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has had watery diarrhoea and bloating for 5 weeks since a holiday in rural Mexico. Two routine stool cultures were negative. She has lost 3 kg. Coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Persistent post-travel diarrhoea with bloating and negative cultures suggests Giardia, which is found by stool microscopy for cysts and PCR.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Two routine stool cultures were negative
steps.x: Persistent diarrhoea after travel with **negative cultures**: think of a parasite such as **Giardia**.

elim: Old test for colonic structure; not useful for infection.
Used for typhoid, which gives fever.
Invasive; stool PCR and microscopy for parasites come first.
Looks for bacterial overgrowth or lactose intolerance, not parasites.

steps.x: **E. Stool microscopy, culture and PCR.** When culture is negative, stool microscopy and PCR find parasites like Giardia.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with C. difficile infection on day 3 of oral vancomycin develops abdominal distension and pain. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. Bowel sounds are reduced. Her white cell count is 24 x10^9/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Distension with systemic toxicity in C. difficile suggests toxic megacolon, so an abdominal X-ray is needed to look for colonic dilation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
C. difficile with **distension** and toxicity: worry about **toxic megacolon**.

elim: Contraindicated in a possibly dilated, inflamed colon.
Risk of perforating an inflamed, dilated colon.
Adds nothing; she already has known colitis.
The organism is already known.

steps.x: **A. Abdominal X-ray.** Distended abdomen in C. difficile: abdominal X-ray for toxic megacolon; avoid endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man in hospital has C. difficile infection confirmed by stool toxin. He is confused, his temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 86/54 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Lactate is 4.1 mmol/L. IV fluids have been started.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: First-line C. difficile treatment is oral vancomycin with fluids; when the patient is septic, IV metronidazole is added.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
He is **septic** (hypotension, raised lactate, confusion) with C. difficile.

elim: IV vancomycin does not reach the colonic lumen, so it does not treat C. difficile.
Fluoroquinolones are a cause of C. difficile, not a treatment.
Second line, for relapse; not the septic regimen.
Not first line, and inadequate in sepsis.

steps.x: **E. Oral vancomycin plus IV metronidazole.** C. difficile: oral vancomycin; septic, add IV metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman on day 5 of IV co-amoxiclav for pneumonia develops 6 watery stools a day. Stool is positive for C. difficile toxin. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. She is drinking well. Her pneumonia has improved and the co-amoxiclav is stopped.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: A first episode of C. difficile is treated with oral vancomycin, fluids and isolation, having stopped the causative antibiotic.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A first, non-septic episode of **C. difficile**.

elim: Not excreted into the gut lumen, so it does not reach the infection.
Not a C. difficile treatment.
Reserved for relapse within 12 weeks of a first episode.
Antimotility drugs are avoided; they risk toxic megacolon.

steps.x: **E. Oral vancomycin.** First episode of C. difficile: oral vancomycin, with infection control throughout.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman had C. difficile infection 8 weeks ago, treated with oral vancomycin, and her symptoms resolved. She now has 5 watery stools a day again and stool is positive for C. difficile toxin. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Relapse within 12 weeks of a first C. difficile episode is treated with oral fidaxomicin.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **relapse** within **12 weeks** of the first episode.

elim: Considered after multiple recurrences, not the first relapse.
Added only when septic.
Fluoroquinolones cause C. difficile.
For fulminant disease or toxic megacolon, not a stable relapse.

steps.x: **D. Oral fidaxomicin.** C. difficile relapse within 12 weeks: oral fidaxomicin.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has had foul-smelling watery diarrhoea, bloating and cramps for 4 weeks since a camping trip in the Rocky Mountains, where he drank stream water. Stool PCR is positive for Giardia lamblia. He is eating and drinking normally.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Giardiasis is treated with metronidazole.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Confirmed **Giardia**: one of the specific organisms that needs treating.

elim: Used for some bacterial dysentery, not Giardia.
Treats threadworm and other helminths, not Giardia.
First line for C. difficile.
Giardiasis is one of the infections that needs specific treatment.

steps.x: **C. Metronidazole.** Giardiasis: metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has had repeated vomiting and two episodes of watery diarrhoea since eating a cream cake at a party 2 hours earlier. Several other guests are also unwell. She has no blood in her stool. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. She can keep down small sips.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Staph aureus food poisoning is caused by preformed toxin and is self-limiting, so management is supportive with hydration and electrolytes.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Onset within **2 hours** of dairy food in a group = **Staph aureus toxin**.

elim: Antibiotics are not needed for most food poisoning.
The illness is due to preformed toxin, so anti-staphylococcal antibiotics do not help.
For C. difficile.
Not needed: mild, short-lived and clinically obvious.

steps.x: **C. Oral rehydration and electrolyte replacement.** Staph aureus food poisoning is managed supportively; antibiotics are not used.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has had profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days and cannot keep any fluids down. He is drowsy, with sunken eyes and cool peripheries. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and capillary refill time 5 seconds. Urine output has been minimal today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Severe dehydration with shock and failure to tolerate oral fluid needs IV 0.9% saline; ORS is first line only for those who can drink.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Severe** dehydration with shock and vomiting: oral fluids will fail.

elim: Does not stay in the circulation to restore volume.
Does not treat dehydration and can worsen invasive infection.
First line for most, but he is severely dehydrated and vomiting everything.
No indication of C. difficile.

steps.x: **A. IV 0.9% sodium chloride.** ORS first line; IV 0.9% saline if severely dehydrated.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has had diarrhoea 5 times a day for 2 days after eating undercooked chicken. There is no blood. She is drinking well and passing urine normally. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. She asks for antibiotics to get back to work faster.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Most infectious diarrhoea is self-limiting (NICE gastroenteritis guidance); ORS is first line and antibiotics are reserved for specific organisms or severe bacterial infection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Mild, non-bloody illness in a well patient who can drink.

elim: She is not severely dehydrated.
Antibiotics are not needed for most infectious diarrhoea and add side effects and C. difficile risk.
Used for Giardia or septic C. difficile, not mild food poisoning.
No red flags: mild, short, not bloody and not immunocompromised.

steps.x: **D. Oral rehydration solution and advice.** Most cases: ORS and no antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman in a four-bed bay develops watery diarrhoea and is found to have C. difficile infection. Oral vancomycin is started. Her temperature is 37.4°C and pulse rate 90 bpm. The nurse in charge asks what else should be done now.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Give oral vancomycin to the other patients in the bay
Isolate in a side room with soap and water handwashing
Repeat stool test to confirm clearance
questions.e: Infection control, with isolation and hand hygiene, is essential throughout to prevent spread of C. difficile on the ward.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: what else should be done now
steps.x: C. difficile on a shared ward: the risk now is **spread**.

elim: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water is needed.
Prophylaxis of contacts is not recommended.
Antimotility drugs risk toxic megacolon.
Testing for cure is not useful; toxin can persist.

steps.x: **C. Isolate in a side room with soap and water handwashing.** Infection control (isolation and hand hygiene) throughout; spores need soap and water.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has 10 days of stepwise fever, abdominal pain and splenomegaly after returning from Bangladesh. Blood cultures grow Salmonella typhi. His temperature is 39.4°C and pulse rate 72 bpm. A medical student asks why he has a systemic illness and splenomegaly rather than just diarrhoea.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Direct toxin damage to the spleen
questions.e: Salmonella typhi invades through M cells in Peyer's patches and disseminates in the reticuloendothelial system (liver, spleen, bone marrow), causing systemic fever and splenomegaly.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Typhoid bacteria leave the gut and live in **macrophages** of the liver and spleen.

elim: Typhoid's systemic disease is from dissemination of invading bacteria, not a circulating splenic toxin.
Not the mechanism in typhoid.
Not part of typhoid.
The mechanism of Staph aureus food poisoning.

steps.x: **B. Dissemination via the reticuloendothelial system.** Typhoid: M cells in Peyer's patches, then reticuloendothelial spread.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman develops progressive leg weakness and absent ankle reflexes 2 weeks after Campylobacter jejuni enteritis. Nerve conduction studies show demyelination. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Her consultant explains that her immune response to the bacterium has damaged her nerves.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Antibodies against Campylobacter lipooligosaccharides cross-react with gangliosides on peripheral nerve myelin: molecular mimicry causes Guillain-Barré syndrome.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Antibodies made against the bacterium attack **myelin**.

elim: Campylobacter does not infect nerves.
The mechanism of serum sickness and some vasculitis.
Botulism, which gives descending paralysis.
Gives a slow subacute neuropathy, not this.

steps.x: **C. Molecular mimicry.** Campylobacter to GBS: molecular mimicry, lipooligosaccharide antibodies cross-react with nerve gangliosides.

questions.stem: A family develops severe vomiting 2 hours after eating rice pudding that had stood at room temperature overnight. The pudding had been thoroughly reboiled before serving. Food samples grow Staphylococcus aureus. The children's temperatures are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason that reboiling did not prevent the illness?
o: The bacteria invade gut mucosa via M cells
The bacteria multiply in the gut after ingestion
The toxin acts through molecular mimicry
questions.e: Staph aureus food poisoning is caused by a preformed, heat-stable enterotoxin in the food, so reheating does not destroy it, and symptoms begin within 1–6 hours.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely reason that reboiling did not prevent the illness? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Short onset and survival of **boiling**: the toxin is already made and heat-stable.

elim: Staph aureus does not form spores; spore formers include Bacillus and Clostridium.
That is Salmonella typhi.
The illness is from preformed toxin, not active infection, hence the very short incubation.
That explains Campylobacter and Guillain-Barré syndrome.

steps.x: **D. The enterotoxin is heat-stable.** Staph aureus: preformed heat-stable enterotoxin, onset 1–6 hours.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with C. difficile infection undergoes flexible sigmoidoscopy. It shows multiple raised yellow plaques, 2 to 8 mm across, on an inflamed colonic mucosa. Biopsy shows epithelial cell death with an overlying layer of fibrin, mucus and inflammatory cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this damage?
o: Toxins A and B disrupting the epithelial cytoskeleton
questions.e: C. difficile toxins A and B disrupt the colonic epithelial cytoskeleton, causing cell death, fluid secretion and pseudomembranes.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of this damage? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Yellow plaques = **pseudomembranes**; they come from toxin-mediated cell death.

elim: Autoimmunity, not C. difficile injury.
The route of Salmonella typhi.
Ischaemic colitis.
Staph aureus food poisoning.

steps.x: **E. Toxins A and B disrupting the epithelial cytoskeleton.** C. difficile: toxins A and B, cytoskeleton damage, pseudomembranous colitis.
